title: Not by an inferior teacher
theme: Taught by an inferior man, the self is not easily known; taught by one ‘not other’, the wandering ends; it is subtler than the subtle and beyond reasoning.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «मनुष्येण»; Raṅgarāmānuja: «देहात्माभिमानिना», one who takes the body for the self
Śaṅkara: «एषः आत्मा यं त्वं मां पृच्छसि»

words.gram: pres. participle passive, m. nom. sg.

words.meaning: when taught by one who is not other
not to be reached by reasoning

sandhi.rule: a + a give ā, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before e; eṣaḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: proktaḥ before e: the visarga becomes y, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य). eṣaḥ drops its visarga before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि).
gatiḥ before a vowel shows r (the visarga after i comes from s, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)). na + asti: P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः).

sandhi.type: yaṇ; final m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: hi + a: i becomes y before a vowel, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). atarkyam keeps its m before a.

sandhi_exceptions.note: nāsti aṇīyān: i before a is not turned into y. The words close the third pāda and open the fourth, and both syllables are counted (11 + 11). GRETIL writes nāsty aṇīyān (corrections.json), which, read as written, would leave the third pāda with 10.

samasa.meaning: taught by one who is not other; Śaṅkara also reads it as ‘the non-other [self] being taught’, «स्वात्मभूते अनन्यस्मिन् आत्मनि प्रोक्ते»
than what has the measure of an atom

morphology.note: pra + ukta, past participle of vac ‘speak’ (vac > uc-): ‘proclaimed, taught’.
Comparative of aṇu ‘minute’ in -īyas: ‘more minute’, with the ablative of comparison aṇupramāṇāt: ‘subtler than the subtlest measure’.

A gerundive of tark ‘reason, conjecture’ with the negative a-: ‘not to be reasoned out’. It is neuter, though the self (eṣaḥ) is masculine; Śaṅkara restates it in the masculine, «अतर्क्यम् अतर्क्यः», and Raṅgarāmānuja makes the self’s nature its subject, «तत्स्वरूपं तर्कागोचरम्».
Present passive participle of cint ‘think’ (tenth class): ‘being thought of [variously]’ — the reason why the self taught by an inferior teacher is not easily known.

translation.literal: ‘This [self], taught by an inferior man, is not easily known well, being thought of in many ways. When it is taught by one who is not other, there is no [further] going here; for it is subtler than the atomic in measure, not to be reasoned out.’
translation.readable: ‘Taught by an ordinary person, this self is not easily understood, for people think of it in so many ways. But when someone who is one with it teaches it, there is no more wandering about it; for it is subtler than the subtlest thing, and beyond the reach of argument.’

anvaya: अवरेण नरेण प्रोक्तः एषः, बहुधा चिन्त्यमानः, सुविज्ञेयः न [भवति] । अनन्यप्रोक्ते अत्र गतिः न अस्ति । [एषः] हि अणुप्रमाणात् अणीयान्, अतर्क्यम् [च] ।
syntax: Three statements. The first is negative, with the participle proktaḥ giving the condition and cintyamānaḥ the reason. The second is a locative absolute (ananyaprokte) with a short main clause, gatir atra nāsti, whose sense depends on how the compound and gati are read. The third (hi) gives the reason for both: the self is subtler than the subtle and beyond reasoning.

ambiguities.topic: ananyaprokte gatir atra nāsti — Śaṅkara’s three readings
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara gives three. (1) When it is taught by a teacher who sees no difference, «अनन्येन अपृथग्दर्शिनाचार्येण प्रतिपाद्यब्रह्मात्मभूतेन प्रोक्ते», there is no more ‘going’, that is, speculation whether it is or is not: «अनेकधा अस्तिनास्तीत्यादिलक्षणा चिन्ता गतिः». (2) When the self, not other than oneself, is taught, there is no other thing to know, «अन्यावगतिर्नास्ति ज्ञेयस्यान्यस्याभावात्», or no more going round in births: «संसारगतिर्वात्र नास्त्यनन्य आत्मनि प्रोक्ते». (3) Reading agatiḥ: there is no failure to understand, «अगतिः अनवबोधोऽपरिज्ञानमत्र नास्ति».

Raṅgarāmānuja: taught by one who is devoted solely to the self taught and has realised it, «उच्यमानात्मनोऽनन्येन तदेकान्तिना ब्रह्मात्मसाक्षात्कारिणा», the understanding that results is not found when an inferior man teaches. He adds two more readings — no wandering in worldly existence, «अत्र = संसारे, गतिः - चङ्क्रमणं नास्तीत्यर्थः», or no understanding when one teaches oneself, «अनन्यप्रोक्ते - स्वयमवगते» — and a variant text anyaprokte, ‘taught by another [inferior man]’: «अन्यप्रोक्ते इति पाठे».

Madhva reverses the sense of ananya: the ‘non-other’ is the one who does not know that the Lord and the self are different, «अन्यो भगवानन्योऽहमित्यजानन्ननन्यः»; taught by such a one, there is no knowledge, «तेन प्रोक्ते गतिर्ज्ञानं नास्ति». His text also reads nareṇāvaraḥ, sujñeyo and gatir asya (corrections.json).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 22 syllables (11 + 11), regular, with the hiatus nāsti aṇīyān at the pāda boundary counted as written.

beginner: Death explains why the right teacher matters. If an ordinary person teaches about the self — someone who has only read or heard about it — the pupil will not understand it well, because people have so many conflicting opinions about it: that it exists or not, that it acts or not, and so on. But when the teacher is one who is truly at one with what he teaches, the pupil’s wandering between opinions comes to an end. Why can a teacher not be replaced by clever thinking? Because the self is finer than the finest thing, and argument alone cannot reach it: one person argues for something small, and another argues for something smaller still, and there is no end. The three commentators disagree sharply on who the right teacher is.
analogy: Like learning a path through a marsh: a guide who has only read maps will argue about the way, while one who has walked it simply leads.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the self, taught by an inferior man, is not easily known, because people think of it in many ways; that when it is taught by ‘one who is not other’ there is no further ‘going’; and that it is subtler than the subtle and beyond reasoning.

commentary.q: Why is it not known when an inferior man teaches it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: because disputants think of it in many ways — «बहुधा अस्ति नास्ति कर्ताकर्ता शुद्धोऽशुद्ध इत्याद्यनेकधा चिन्त्यमानः वादिभिः». The ‘inferior man’ is one of ordinary understanding, «हीनेन प्राकृतबुद्धिनेत्येतत्». The knowledge of the self’s oneness is the final end of knowledge: «ज्ञानस्य ह्येषा परा निष्ठा यदात्मैकत्वविज्ञानम्».

commentary.q: Why can reasoning not reach it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: if one person establishes the self as atomic, another reasons it subtler still, and another subtler again; reasoning has no resting place, «न हि तर्कस्य निष्ठा क्वचिद्विद्यते». Raṅgarāmānuja: since the self is subtler than the subtle, its nature is beyond the reach of reasoning: «यतोऽणोरप्यणीयान् आत्मा, अतः तत्स्वरूपं तर्कागोचरम्».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: For Śaṅkara, a teacher who sees no difference and is one with the Brahman he teaches: «अपृथग्दर्शिनाचार्येण प्रतिपाद्यब्रह्मात्मभूतेन». For Raṅgarāmānuja, one devoted solely to the self taught, who has realised it: «तदेकान्तिना ब्रह्मात्मसाक्षात्कारिणा». For Madhva the ‘non-other’ is precisely the one who does not know the difference between the Lord and himself, and from him no knowledge comes: «अन्यो भगवानन्योऽहमित्यजानन्ननन्यः». He supports this from the next verse, «प्रोक्ताऽन्येनैव सुज्ञानाय प्रेष्ठ इति वाक्यशेषात्», and cites the Brahmavaivarta: «जीवानां चैव विष्णोश्च यो न वेत्ति भिदां पुमान्».

advaita.text: Taught by a teacher who is himself the Brahman he teaches, the self leaves nothing further to know and no further birth: «अतः गन्तव्याभावान्न गतिरत्रावशिष्यते».

visistadvaita.text: The teacher who is ‘not other’ is wholly devoted to the self he teaches and has seen it: «तदेकान्तिना ब्रह्मात्मसाक्षात्कारिणा». An inferior teacher is one who takes the body for the self, «देहात्माभिमानिना».

dvaita.text: The ‘non-other’ is the one who does not know that the Lord is other and the self other; taught by him there is no knowledge: «तेन प्रोक्ते गतिर्ज्ञानं नास्ति». The next verse, ‘taught by another’, completes the sense.

schools.disagreement: The verse is one of the sharpest points of disagreement in the Kaṭha. For Śaṅkara the ‘non-other’ teacher is the one who knows non-difference, and his teaching ends all difference; for Raṅgarāmānuja he is one wholly devoted to the self he has realised; for Madhva the ‘non-other’ is one who denies the difference between the Lord and the self, and from such a teacher no knowledge comes.

parallels.note: Death will soon describe the self as ‘subtler than the subtle’; aṇīyān … aṇupramāṇāt here anticipates it.
‘To know it, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman.’ The Muṇḍaka also makes the right teacher the condition of the knowledge.
Śaṅkara’s Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya makes the same argument as his comment here: reasoning without scripture rests on individual conjecture and has no firm ground.

contemporary.text: In many fields there are two kinds of teacher: one who has collected opinions about a subject and one who has lived inside it. The first can make a subject seem endlessly debatable; the second can end a student’s confusion with a few words. The verse adds a warning about argument: on some questions, cleverness only produces a more refined version of the last guess. This is a reflection, not part of the commentaries.

reflect.beginner: Who have you learned from who seemed to know a subject from the inside?
reflect.deeper: Why might more argument make some questions harder rather than easier?
reflect.practice: Before your next argument about something important, ask yourself whether you have experience of it, or only opinions.

flags.note: ananyaprokte: taught by a teacher who knows non-difference (Śaṅkara), by one devoted to and realising the self (Raṅgarāmānuja), or — reversing the sense — by one who denies the difference of Lord and self, from whom no knowledge comes (Madhva).
Madhva’s text reads nareṇāvaraḥ, sujñeyo and gatir asya; Raṅgarāmānuja reports a reading anyaprokte (corrections.json; his comment).
